title: Potential end of US aid to Peshmerga could mark 'transitional phase' in US-KRG relations, experts say
gist: Washington is expected to end up to $61 million a year in aid to the Kurdish Peshmerga on Sept. 30, alongside the wind-down of the US-led anti-ISIS coalition mission in Iraq. Experts read it less as a rupture than a transitional phase that pushes Erbil toward Baghdad for funding and leaves the KRG's air-defense gap against Iranian and militia drones as the binding security problem.

insights.claim: US financial assistance to Iraqi Kurdish Peshmerga forces of up to $61 million a year is reported to end on Sept. 30, 2026.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A dated, quantified fiscal cliff for Erbil's security budget; watch KRG-Baghdad salary transfers around Q4.
insights.quote: US support, including up to $61 million in annual financial assistance to Peshmerga forces, is expected to end on Sept. 30.
insights.locator: According to reports by the BBC and local media

insights.claim: The Peshmerga aid cutoff coincides with the expected conclusion of the US-led Global Coalition Against Daesh mission in Iraq, meaning funding and force presence unwind together.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Two withdrawals stacking on one date raises the odds of a security gap in northern Iraq in late 2026.
insights.locator: The reported date for the potential end of assistance

insights.claim: The Peshmerga aid was always tied to the anti-ISIS mission framework and was never designed to be permanent, with the coalition's combat mission having formally ended back in December 2021.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Frames the cutoff as scheduled normalization rather than a Trump-era abandonment signal; avoid over-trading the headline.
insights.quote: From the start, this aid was provided under the framework of the anti-ISIS mission that’s now ending and was never going to be permanent
insights.locator: KRG to become more dependent on Baghdad

insights.claim: The most urgent security requirement for Iraqi Kurds is acquiring air defense capable of stopping drone and missile attacks by Iran and allied militias, a gap that widens as the last US troops and their systems leave.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Creates a concrete demand signal for short-range air defense and counter-drone systems in northern Iraq if Erbil seeks substitutes.
insights.quote: Combined with the loss of US systems as the US pulls its last remaining troops, ending the aid program would make the KRG more vulnerable to attacks
insights.locator: ‘Would make KRG more vulnerable to attacks’

insights.claim: The withdrawal of coalition forces will hit Kurdistan Regional Government security harder than the end of the aid money, at least in the immediate term, because American and British air defense systems that protected Erbil during the US/Israel-Iran war are now being pulled out.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The tradable variable is hardware presence, not the $61 million line item; track coalition system departures rather than aid headlines.
insights.quote: The withdrawal of coalition forces will impact KRG security more than the end of the aid, at least in the immediate term
insights.locator: Coalition withdrawal may have greater impact

insights.claim: Coalition air defenses never provided strategic protection for the Kurdish region: Peshmerga members were killed in missile strikes during the war, KRG leaders' residences were repeatedly hit by drones, and coalition forces could not or did not stop IRGC missile attacks on Erbil in 2022 and 2024.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Tempers the assumption that US presence was ever an effective insurance policy for assets in Erbil, including oil operations.
insights.quote: never provided a strategic defense for the KRG
insights.locator: Nevertheless, Iddon stressed that the systems

insights.claim: Even after withdrawal, US and coalition fighter jets flying from bases outside Iraq are expected to keep occasionally shooting down Iraqi militia and Iranian drones over the Kurdish region, a pattern already visible in recent months.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Over-the-horizon coverage caps but does not eliminate tail risk to northern Iraq energy and expatriate operations.
insights.quote: I think after the withdrawal, you will still see US/coalition fighter jets flying from bases outside Iraq occasionally shooting down Iraqi militia and Iranian drones targeting the region
insights.locator: Coalition withdrawal may have greater impact

themes.theme: Leverage shifts to Baghdad and Tehran

insights.claim: Iraqi Kurdish parties need Washington more than Washington needs them, so the end of Peshmerga aid is unlikely to fundamentally change US-KRG relations.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Asymmetric dependence means Erbil absorbs the cut rather than realigning; discount narratives of a US-KRG rupture.
insights.quote: At the end of the day, the Kurdish parties in Iraq need the US more than the US needs them
insights.locator: Aid assistance 'was never a long-term setup'

insights.claim: Ending US assistance could force the Kurdistan Regional Government to take security-sector reform seriously and to coordinate more closely with Baghdad-led federal security forces.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A federal-integration path for the Peshmerga would reshape Erbil-Baghdad bargaining over budgets and oil revenue.
insights.locator: Aid assistance 'was never a long-term setup'

insights.claim: US presence and support did not prevent attacks by Iran and armed groups in Iraq, so a smaller US footprint may remove a pretext for targeting the Kurdish region.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Argues US drawdown can lower rather than raise attack frequency on Erbil, the opposite of the consensus risk read.
insights.quote: US presence and support hasn’t prevented attacks from Iran and armed groups in Iraq, (so) with less US involvement then there will be less of an excuse for KRG to be a target
insights.locator: Aid assistance 'was never a long-term setup'

insights.claim: Erbil, which has long struggled to pay most civil servant salaries on time, will become even more dependent on Baghdad to fund Peshmerga troops employed by the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Adds payroll stress to an already fragile KRG fiscal position and gives Baghdad added leverage in revenue disputes.
insights.quote: will become even more dependent on Baghdad to fund these Peshmerga troops employed by the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs
insights.locator: KRG to become more dependent on Baghdad

insights.claim: With less US backing, the Kurdistan Regional Government could face growing Iranian pressure on issues such as the presence of Kurdish opposition groups on its territory.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Watch Iranian demands as a leading indicator of how far Tehran's influence extends into northern Iraq post-drawdown.
insights.locator: ‘Would make KRG more vulnerable to attacks’

insights.claim: Iraqi Kurdish leaders read the 2025-2026 conflicts, in which the US appeared to abandon Syrian Kurds in favor of strengthening Syria's post-Assad central government, as a template for how Washington may treat them.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Allied-hedging behavior in the region tends to follow perceived US abandonment precedents; expect more Erbil outreach to Ankara, Baghdad and Gulf states.

insights.claim: US officials point to the newly built largest American consulate in Erbil as evidence of continued ties, while a potential power vacuum in Iraq remains the main worry for the Kurdish leadership.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Diplomatic infrastructure suggests the US is restructuring rather than exiting; the risk to price is an Iraqi power vacuum, not a US departure.
insights.quote: US officials keep pointing to the fact that the largest American consulate was just built here in Erbil as a testament to continued ties. Still, a potential power vacuum in Iraq is worrying for KRG

insights.claim: The likely end state is a transitional phase in which Washington and Erbil operate under a new security framework rather than a termination of the relationship.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Sets up a replacement bilateral arrangement as the base case to watch for in late 2026 and 2027.
insights.locator: New security framework possible between US and KRG
